answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 all three catalytic domains sit in one superfamily: c.55.1 "Actin-like ATPase domain" (sunid 53067), in fold c.55 "Ribonuclease H-like motif" and class c (alpha and beta proteins, a/b). They are separate families within that superfamily: Actin/HSP70 is c.55.1.1 (sunid 53068), Hexokinase is c.55.1.3 (53083), and Glycerol kinase is c.55.1.4 (53089). Other families in c.55.1 include acetokinase-like, glucokinase, ROK, BadF/BadG, Ppx/GppA and NTPDase-like. So SCOPe places them at the superfamily level, meaning a distant but evolutionarily supported (common ancestry) relationship from structural and functional evidence. It is not a family-level, close-sequence relationship. The superfamily is annotated as containing a duplication, with two domains of this fold. What you can infer: (1) they very likely descend from a common ancestor and share the conserved two-lobe core, a nucleotide/ATP-binding cleft and a phosphoryl-transfer architecture. This is consistent with their shared ATP-dependent chemistry and with very different cellular roles arising by divergence (cytoskeletal actin, HSP70 chaperone, sugar kinase, glycerol kinase). (2) You can use one as a structural template for the shared core fold, and the conserved ATP-binding region, only with care. What you cannot infer: the same specific function, substrate, or mechanism; family-level homology (they are different families, with low sequence identity); transfer of functional annotation or catalytic residues; or that loops, insertions, and interdomain orientation or ligand-binding sites are conserved. Sharing the c.55 fold alone would not establish homology, but the superfamily assignment does. Even so, homology here supports only the common-core inference. Substrate specificity and biological role must be checked with family-specific evidence, such as sequence conservation, active-site residues and experimental data.

answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 all three catalytic domains sit in one superfamily: c.55.1 "Actin-like ATPase domain" (sunid 53067), in fold c.55 "Ribonuclease H-like motif" and class c (alpha and beta proteins, a/b). They are separate families within that superfamily: Actin/HSP70 is c.55.1.1 (sunid 53068), Hexokinase is c.55.1.3 (53083), and Glycerol kinase is c.55.1.4 (53089). Other families in c.55.1 include acetokinase-like, glucokinase, ROK, BadF/BadG, Ppx/GppA and NTPDase-like. So SCOPe places them at the superfamily level, meaning a distant but evolutionarily supported (common ancestry) relationship from structural and functional evidence. It is not a family-level, close-sequence relationship. The superfamily is annotated as containing a duplication, with two domains of this fold. What you can infer: (1) they very likely descend from a common ancestor and share the conserved two-lobe core, a nucleotide/ATP-binding cleft and a phosphoryl-transfer architecture. This is consistent with their shared ATP-dependent chemistry and with very different cellular roles arising by divergence (cytoskeletal actin, HSP70 chaperone, sugar kinase, glycerol kinase). (2) You can use one as a structural template for the shared core fold, and the conserved ATP-binding region, only with care. What you cannot infer: the same specific function, substrate, or mechanism; family-level homology (they are different families, with low sequence identity); transfer of functional annotation or catalytic residues; or that loops, insertions, and interdomain orientation or ligand-binding sites are conserved. Sharing the c.55 fold alone would not establish homology, but the superfamily assignment does. Even so, homology here supports only the common-core inference. Substrate specificity and biological role must be checked with family-specific evidence, such as sequence conservation, active-site residues and experimental data.
